newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: New truce deal in Central Africa, capital empties.
newsitem.headline: New truce deal in Central Africa, capital empties.

text.p: Army mutineers and loyalist soldiers have agreed to extend a ceasefire in fighting in the Central African Republic capital Bangui, a presidential spokesman said on Sunday.
The breakthrough was announced as thousands of Bangui residents fled to the countryside ahead of Sunday's expiry of a 15-day ceasefire brokered by four African presidents.
Residents reckon the city of 600,000 people has been emptied of about a third of its population since the mutiny that erupted on November 16 degenerated into tribal bloodletting.
"The two sides will sign this afternoon for the extension of the truce," spokesman Theophile Doumba told Reuters. He said the length of the extension had not been decided.

The latest agreement follows more than a week of difficult mediation by former Malian military ruler General Amadou Toumani Toure, who had been joined later by the French ambassador, sources close to the talks said.

French troops based in the former colony under bilateral accords helped keep President Ange-Felix Patasse in power during a violent mutiny last May and have been backing loyalist forces in the latest revolt.

Mutineers with pay grievances later started demanding that Patasse step down. Patasse was elected 1993 and has dismissed calls for his resignation, backed by the opposition, as unconstitutional. The mutiny has turned into bloody feuding between his Baya tribe and Yakomas who dominate the ranks of rebel soldiers.
Mutineers accuse Patasse of arming his civilian supporters and of hiring mercenaries from Chad and Sudan. The rebels have vowed to forcibly disarm Patasse loyalists, stoking tension.
The two principal roads leading out of Bangui have been choked with residents heading to their home provinces in buses, trucks and whatever other means. Some are forced to walk.
"In many households nine out of 10 family members have left. The city has emptied and only working men remain behind," one resident said.

"My house has just been destroyed by the military. What I want to do now is leave Bangui forever. I have never seen such violence in 40 years," said Daniel Demba, loading his belongings on a truck at the Kilometre Five motor park.
Several houses have been hit in the cross-fire of rocket propelled grenades in battles between the two sides. It has not always been possible to determine which side caused the damage.
Museum worker Cecile Dounia said he had decided to take his family home and wait out the situation before returning himself to the capital.
"In Miskine district where I live arms have been distributted to supporters of the regime," he said. "I no longer have hope for peace in this country after three mutinies."

Soldiers earlier revolted in April and May over pay and status. French troops using helicopter gunships and armoured vehicles clashed with rebels in May before Patasse agreed concessions that ended the uprising for a period.
